title: Karkotaka's bite
hook: Nala carries a snake king out of a fire, and its bite starts driving out the Kali inside him
carry: reciting nala's story is a prayer against kali

segments.voice: Yesterday: ashoka, the tree whose name means without sorrow, and Damayanti alone in the forest with nothing but her dharma. Your line was dharma protects the one who protects it.

A voice in a forest fire. Nala, wandering alone after leaving Damayanti, hears someone calling his name out of the flames. Come quickly, Nala. He follows the voice and finds, curled in the fire, a great serpent. It's Karkotaka, a king among the nagas, and he can't move: a sage's curse has frozen him there until Nala comes to carry him. So the man who lost everything at dice lifts a snake king onto his shoulder and walks out of the fire. And then the snake bites him.
screen: `A VOICE IN THE FIRE.` → `KARKOTAKA, THE SERPENT KING.` → `THEN THE SNAKE BITES HIM.`

segments.voice: Nala's body changes. His beauty is gone; no one would know him now. And Karkotaka explains: my poison won't hurt you. It will torment the one living inside you, the one who brought all this on you. That's Kali. Not the goddess Kali; a different name. This Kali is the spirit of quarrel and bad luck, the same name Hindus give our whole age, the Kali Yuga. Then the serpent gives Nala a plan. Go to King Rituparna of Ayodhya. Call yourself Vahuka and drive his horses, and he'll teach you his secret of dice. And take this garment: when you want your own shape back, put it on and think of me. So the king becomes a charioteer. Every evening he recites a lament for a woman left alone in a forest. Meanwhile, Damayanti has been found and brought home to her father's house and her children. She sends Brahmanas out with one question for every court: where did you go, gambler, after you cut your sleeping wife's cloth? Now the teaching. With this story comes a short Sanskrit verse, still recited, that names four people: Karkotaka the serpent, Damayanti, Nala, and the royal sage Rituparna. Naming them, it says, destroys Kali. Notice who comes first: the snake whose bite began to drive Kali out. Some Hindus still say the verse in a hard season, a lost job, an illness, a run of bad luck. For today: in this tradition, a story isn't only something you hear. Said with faith, it's a prayer.
screen: `THE BITE THAT HIDES HIM.` · `KALI, THE SPIRIT OF BAD LUCK.` · `NALA BECOMES VAHUKA.` · `FOUR NAMES THAT DRIVE OUT KALI.` · then, large: `A STORY, SAID AS A PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Say the four names of the verse slowly, one on each breath out: Karkotaka. Damayanti. Nala. Rituparna. Let each one bring back a piece of the story: the bite, the search, the hiding, the secret of dice. If you pray, hold a hard season of your own, or someone else's, in that prayer; if not, simply bring to mind the people who carried you through one.
Karkotaka. The naga king whose bite hid Nala and tormented Kali, and the first name in the verse said against Kali.
Your line: reciting Nala's story is a prayer against Kali. A snake king, named first. Day seven hundred ninety-three, done.

howItsDone: In the Mahabharata's Nala story, the serpent Karkotaka disguises Nala and torments Kali inside him; a verse with the story names Karkotaka, Damayanti, Nala and Rituparna as destroying Kali, and some Hindus still recite it in hard times.
